doc: PTO, the PhoTon cOntainer, and the targeted reads of PRD-020. The container's whole claim on the read side is that reading part of it costs the part -- a column subset of an embedded table, a row window of one, a byte range of any payload, a range of events in a photon stream. That claim has to hold in every binding, because the reason a container exists is that the file outlives the program that wrote it.

cases.doc: The container round trip, reduced to something comparable: what went in, listed by name and kind after the file was closed and reopened.

args: instrument bytes, all forty of them

unsupported.r: a 64-bit FileUID does not survive this binding's native number, so a uid read here is a nearby value rather than that uid and cannot be handed back. Every case in this area binds a uid and passes it on. R's numeric is a double and base R has no 64-bit integer; JavaScript's Number is a double and only 64-bit ARRAYS cross as BigInt today (see ext/js/jsarrays.i). Python's int and Java's BigInteger both carry it, so the cases still run in two bindings.

cases.doc: PRD-020 part 1. An embedded store is always a region of a bigger file, so before pto_read_store took a column list a caller could ask for a subset of a store's columns OR for a store inside a container, never both -- and the container only ever produces the second.

cases.doc: PRD-020 part 3, and what a table viewer needs: paging a table used to decode all of it to show a page. The window is a projection along the other axis from a column subset, and dictionary-encoded text is the case that can be got wrong -- the codes are sliced and the dictionary is not.

cases.doc: PRD-020 part 4. A real instrument file embedded in a container, indexed with cues, then read in the middle. Macro times are the check that matters: a decode starting at a cue has no idea how many overflows preceded it, and the cue's own macro time is the only thing that closes the gap.
